headline: Schindler says he suspects he has ADHD
standfirst: After reaching the Grand Slam last 16, Martin Schindler said his mental game may need more than a mental coach and that he has never been formally diagnosed.
body: Martin Schindler's interview after beating Chris Dobey at the Grand Slam of Darts attracted as much attention as the result. The German number one, through to the last 16, spoke openly about the thoughts that run through his head while he plays.

Asked whether he had considered a mental coach during a dip in form earlier this season, Schindler said he felt his situation might be more a matter for a therapist. He stressed he has no diagnosis, having never seen a doctor about it, but said he is "pretty certain" he has ADHD.

He said a mental coach would help with resetting after an opponent's good moment or his own weak one, but he sees his challenge as deeper than that. In matches, he explained, he can find himself wondering about almost anything, from why an opponent's first dart landed where it did to why a visit scored only 41.

Schindler said he tries to stay in the moment and believes he needs to be a little more himself on stage. He added that he does not want to smile constantly like some other players, but thinks a smile suits a funny situation.

He also described how he separates darts from family life. He once told his wife he wanted no dartboard in the living room, he said, but that is now where it hangs. He wants home to be private time with his wife and child, although sponsors, exhibitions and other events mean darts is never far away.
Schindler was pleased with his group-stage focus and body language. He plays Gian van Veen in the last 16 on Thursday.
